introduction_markdown:
**Time allowed: three hours.** This paper contains six questions arranged in three sections: Section A - Physical and General Chemistry (questions 1 and 2); Section B - Inorganic Chemistry (questions 3 and 4); Section C - Organic Chemistry (questions 5 and 6).

Answer ALL the SIX questions in this booklet. The mark allocation is indicated for each question. Each question carries 20 marks. In calculations you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. All necessary working must be shown. No marks will be awarded for answers without brief statements showing how the answers have been obtained. Calculators may be used.

**Useful data:** one atmosphere (1 atm) = 1 Pa = $1.01\times10^{5}$ N m$^{-2}$ (as printed); relative atomic masses (RAM): C = 12.0, S = 32.0, O = 16.0, H = 1.0; molar gas volume at stp = 22400 cm$^3$.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Iron and manganese are transition metals.

(i) Define a transition metal.

(ii) Using the boxes below, write out the electronic configuration for $\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ ion (Mn = 25, Fe = 26).

| Ion | 3d orbitals (to be filled in) |
|---|---|
| ${}_{26}\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ | [Ar] followed by five empty boxes labelled 3d |
| ${}_{25}\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$ | [Ar] followed by five empty boxes labelled 3d |

(iii) Account for the fact that $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ ions are readily oxidized to $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$ ions but $\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$ ions are not readily oxidized to $\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}$. *[5 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** A transition metal is a **d-block element that forms at least one stable ion with a partially filled d sub-shell** (e.g. iron forms $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$, $3d^6$, and $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$, $3d^5$).

**(ii)** Here $[\mathrm{Ar}] = 1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^6$. The neutral atoms are $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^6\,4s^2$ (Fe) and $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^5\,4s^2$ (Mn); the 4s electrons are lost first, so the 4s sub-shell is empty in both ions. Electrons are placed singly in the five 3d orbitals first (Hund's rule), with parallel spins:

| Ion | Configuration | 3d boxes |
|---|---|---|
| ${}_{26}\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ | $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^6$ | [↑↓] [↑] [↑] [↑] [↑] |
| ${}_{25}\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$ | $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^5$ | [↑] [↑] [↑] [↑] [↑] |

**(iii)** Oxidation of $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ to $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$ removes one electron from $3d^6$ and gives $3d^5$, a **half-filled d sub-shell**, which is particularly stable (each orbital singly occupied with parallel spins: extra exchange energy and a symmetrical electron distribution). The third ionisation energy of iron is therefore relatively low and $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ is easily oxidised (for $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}}$, $E^\circ \approx +0.77\ \mathrm{V}$).

$\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$ is **already $3d^5$** (half-filled and stable). Oxidation to $\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}$ would break this arrangement and give $3d^4$, so the third ionisation energy of manganese is very high and only a very strong oxidising agent can do it ($E^\circ(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}/Mn^{2+}}) \approx +1.5\ \mathrm{V}$). $\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$ is therefore not readily oxidised.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Give the transition metal or transition metal compound used as catalyst in the following conversions.

(i) $\mathrm{N_2(g)} + 3\mathrm{H_2(g)} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{NH_3(g)}$

(ii) $2\mathrm{SO_2(g)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{SO_3(g)}$ *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** Haber process: **iron** (finely divided Fe, usually with $\mathrm{K_2O}$/$\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$ promoters), at about 450 $^\circ$C and 200 atm.

**(ii)** Contact process: **vanadium(V) oxide**, $\mathrm{V_2O_5}$, at about 450 $^\circ$C and 1-2 atm.

Both are heterogeneous catalysts: reactant molecules adsorb on the surface (using the partly filled d orbitals or variable oxidation states), react, and desorb.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The group I and II elements are called s-block elements.

(i) State and explain the general trend of the reaction of the elements down group I and II with water.

(ii) Give the formula of an s-block oxide which is amphoteric.

(iii) Write out balanced chemical reactions of the amphoteric oxide in c(ii) with HCl and NaOH.

(iv) State and explain the trend in the solubility of the s-block sulphates down the groups. *[7 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Trend:** the reactivity with water **increases down both groups**.

- Group I: lithium reacts steadily, sodium vigorously (melts to a ball), potassium very vigorously (the hydrogen ignites with a lilac flame): $2\mathrm{M} + 2\mathrm{H_2O} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{MOH} + \mathrm{H_2}$ for M = Li, Na, K.
- Group II: beryllium does not react, magnesium reacts very slowly with cold water but burns in steam ($\mathrm{Mg} + \mathrm{H_2O} \rightarrow \mathrm{MgO} + \mathrm{H_2}$), calcium reacts steadily and strontium and barium vigorously: $\mathrm{Ca} + 2\mathrm{H_2O} \rightarrow \mathrm{Ca(OH)_2} + \mathrm{H_2}$.

**Explanation:** going down a group the atomic radius increases and the outer electrons are more shielded from the nuclear charge, so the ionisation energy decreases (first for Group I; first plus second for Group II). The outer electron(s) are lost more easily, i.e. the metals are stronger reducing agents, so they react more readily with water.

**(ii)** Beryllium oxide, **$\mathrm{BeO}$**.

**(iii)** As a basic oxide it reacts with acid: $\mathrm{BeO} + 2\mathrm{HCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{BeCl_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}$

As an acidic oxide it reacts with alkali to give a beryllate: $\mathrm{BeO} + 2\mathrm{NaOH} + \mathrm{H_2O} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na_2[Be(OH)_4]}$ (sodium tetrahydroxoberyllate); in the anhydrous form, $\mathrm{BeO} + 2\mathrm{NaOH} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na_2BeO_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}$

**(iv)** The solubility of the **Group II sulphates decreases down the group**: $\mathrm{BeSO_4}$ and $\mathrm{MgSO_4}$ are soluble, $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$ is sparingly soluble, $\mathrm{SrSO_4}$ and $\mathrm{BaSO_4}$ are insoluble.

Explanation: the enthalpy change of solution is the energy needed to break up the lattice minus the energy released when the ions are hydrated. The sulphate ion is large, so the lattice enthalpy changes little down the group, whereas the hydration enthalpy of the cation falls markedly as its radius grows (lower charge density). The enthalpy of solution becomes less exothermic (more positive), so solubility falls. (The Group I sulphates are all soluble in water.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
The Group IV (Groups 14) elements of the periodic table are carbon, silicon, germanium, tin and lead.

(i) Give the trend in the structure of the elements from carbon to lead.

(ii) Identify the elements which exhibit allotropy.

Give the allotropes of one of the elements.

(iii) These elements exhibit two oxidation states. Use the oxides of lead to illustrate this property. *[6 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** The structure changes from **giant covalent to giant metallic** down the group: carbon (diamond, graphite) and silicon and germanium (diamond-type lattices) are giant covalent non-metals or metalloids with high melting points and poor (or semi-) conductivity; tin and lead have **giant metallic lattices**, soft, conducting and with low melting points. Metallic character increases down the group.

**(ii)** **Carbon** and **tin** show allotropy (different structural forms of the same element in the same physical state).

Allotropes of carbon: **diamond** (each C bonded tetrahedrally to four others, very hard, insulator), **graphite** (layers of hexagonal rings, soft, conducts electricity) and **fullerenes** (e.g. $\mathrm{C_{60}}$). (Tin: grey $\alpha$-tin, diamond type, and white $\beta$-tin, metallic.)

**(iii)** The elements show the oxidation states **+4** (all four outer electrons used) and **+2** (only the two p electrons used, the s pair stays: the *inert pair effect*, increasingly marked down the group). For lead: **lead(II) oxide, PbO** (Pb is +2, the stable state for lead) and **lead(IV) oxide, $\mathrm{PbO_2}$** (Pb is +4). $\mathrm{PbO_2}$ is a strong oxidising agent because Pb(IV) tends to revert to the stable Pb(II): $\mathrm{PbO_2} + 4\mathrm{HCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{PbCl_2} + \mathrm{Cl_2} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}$. The mixed oxide $\mathrm{Pb_3O_4}$ ($2\mathrm{PbO}\cdot\mathrm{PbO_2}$) contains both states.
